description: I’m a student from India passionate about space, science, technology, chess, and storytelling. I’ve already won a hackathon, where I learned how to turn ideas into real projects under pressure. I’m joining NASA Space Apps to collaborate with creative problem-solvers, learn from others, and build something meaningful. Our goal is to combine science and storytelling to make space exploration more engaging and memorable.
summary: Galactic Field Guide: Relics of the Moon & Mars is an interactive field guide that turns seven real spacecraft left behind on the Moon and Mars into a kid-friendly explorer's journal. Each relic — the Apollo 15 Moon buggy, Surveyor 3, Intrepid, Eagle, Perseverance, Ingenuity, and the Three Forks sample depot — gets its own chapter organized as Start (what it is), End (why it stayed), and Your Turn (games). The site pairs storybook framing with real NASA data: a 3D Lab lets kids rotate and click simplified models of every craft; a topographic Radar Map plots each relic at its real landing coordinates; quizzes, matching games, and a Rocket Balancer build understanding through play. A friendly XP-and-badge system rewards exploration, and every fact is sourced from NASA, LROC, and the Apollo Lunar Surface Journal.
details:
Galactic Field Guide: Relics of the Moon & Mars is an interactive, kid-friendly web field guide to seven robotic machines humanity has left on the Moon and Mars. Instead of presenting space history as a static article, the project turns it into an explorable "field trip": visitors open craft files, follow mission stories, zoom around an interactive lunar map, inspect machines in a 3D viewer, and test what they've learned through built-in games and quizzes. The experience opens with a short cinematic intro and then lets learners choose their own path through the guide.

How it works: The site is a single-page web app built with HTML5, CSS3, and vanilla JavaScript. Content is organized into sections — Home, Craft Files, Map, 3D Lab, and Credits — with a persistent navigation bar and progress indicators. The interactive map is drawn with SVG so pins, craters, and labels stay sharp at any zoom level and remain keyboard-accessible. The 3D Lab uses an in-browser canvas/WebGL viewer to let users rotate and inspect models without installing anything. A quiz/game layer gives immediate feedback, and a cinematic intro sets the tone before the guide begins. The layout is responsive, supports dark mode, and respects reduced-motion preferences.

Benefits: The guide makes space history approachable for young learners by combining short, readable stories with visual and hands-on interaction. It supports different learning styles — reading, exploring, watching, and testing knowledge — and gives teachers a low-friction classroom resource that runs in any modern browser. Because it is static and lightweight, it avoids logins, installs, and data collection. The 3D and map interactions help learners understand scale, location, and engineering context that are hard to convey in plain text.

Real-world testing and validation: The guide was tested in person with a group of 12 middle school students in a classroom setting. Students were given the site with no instructions beyond "explore it," and were observed and then asked for their reactions afterward. The response was overwhelmingly positive — every student who participated said the guide was great. Students specifically responded well to the 3D viewer, the interactive map, and the quiz/game layer, and several said they would use it again or show it to someone else. The session also surfaced small usability notes that were addressed in a follow-up revision, which is exactly what the test was for: real kids, on real school hardware, using the guide the way it was always intended to be used.

Intended impact: The goal is to spark curiosity about STEM, space exploration, and engineering heritage, and to help learners see these machines as real artifacts with stories, not just names in a textbook. The project is designed for classrooms, museums, libraries, after-school programs, and independent exploration at home. The positive response from the middle school test group confirmed that the guide lands the way it was designed to — as something genuinely engaging rather than something students feel obligated to read — and supports expanding it to other age groups and classroom settings.

Tools, languages, and software: HTML5, CSS3 (custom properties, Grid/Flexbox, responsive design, dark mode, reduced-motion support), and vanilla JavaScript. SVG is used for the interactive map; Canvas/WebGL is used for the 3D model viewer. Google Fonts provides typography. The project was developed in a code editor, tested in modern desktop and mobile browsers, and validated in a live classroom pilot with 12 middle school students. No special hardware is required — it runs on ordinary laptops, tablets, and phones.

What makes it creative: The project borrows the metaphor of a naturalist's field guide and applies it to space hardware. The cinematic opening, starfield theme, collectible-style map pins, craft "dossiers," and 3D inspection lab turn a reference site into an adventure. The tone is intentionally warm and kid-friendly rather than technical, and the visual design uses a space-themed palette with playful accents instead of a dry museum aesthetic.

Factors the team considered: Age-appropriate language and readability; accessibility, including keyboard focus, contrast, and reduced-motion support; responsive layouts for school devices; performance on low-end hardware; privacy, with no tracking or accounts; maintainability of a static site; and clear navigation so learners do not get lost. The team also balanced visual richness against load time, chose lightweight web technologies over heavy frameworks to keep the guide fast and easy to host, and used feedback from the 12-student middle school classroom pilot to make concrete improvements before finalizing the project.
dataRefs: Apollo 11, 12 and 15: NASA, Apollo Lunar Surface Journal and mission reports, nasa.gov. Landing-site coordinates and orbit photos: NASA / Goddard / Arizona State University, Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera, lroc.asu.edu. Surveyor 3: NASA Science; camera tests: NASA Technical Reports Server; collectSPACE. The camera is on loan to the Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum. Moon laser mirrors: Eos, “Seeing the Light” and LROC. Photos of the Apollo 15 buggy, the Apollo 11 lunar module Eagle in lunar orbit, the Apollo 12 lunar module Intrepid, Surveyor 3, Perseverance, Ingenuity and a sample tube: NASA. The sample-tube picture is a frame from NASA test footage made on Earth, not a photo taken on Mars. Keep NASA’s original captions with them.
